hints: Look closely at the starting ketone, pentan-3-one, and ask what groups are attached to the carbonyl carbon after addition.
Draw the product as $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{C(OH)(CN)CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ and check if the central carbon has four different groups.
Recall how $\text{HCN}$ actually reacts, with $\text{CN}^-$ attacking first to give a negative oxygen intermediate, then $\text{HCN}$ providing $\text{H}^+$ to regenerate $\text{CN}^-$.
walkthrough:
**Draw the starting ketone and product**

This ketone is pentan-3-one, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COCH}_2\text{CH}_3$. It is symmetrical with an ethyl group on each side of the $\text{C=O}$.

Addition of $\text{HCN}$ across $\text{C=O}$ gives:
$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COCH}_2\text{CH}_3 + \text{HCN} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{C(OH)(CN)CH}_2\text{CH}_3$$

**Test for chirality and type of addition**

The new central carbon is bonded to $\text{OH}$, $\text{CN}$, and two identical $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ groups. With two identical groups it cannot be chiral.

The $\text{C=O}$ carbon is electron poor (delta positive), so it is attacked by the nucleophile $\text{CN}^-$. This is nucleophilic addition, not electrophilic addition.

**Follow the real mechanism**

$\text{CN}^-$ attacks the carbonyl carbon to form an alkoxide intermediate containing $\text{C-O}^-$, not $\text{C-OH}$.
$$\text{R}_2\text{C=O} + \text{CN}^- \rightarrow \text{R}_2\text{C(CN)O}^-$$
The $\text{O}^-$ is protonated by $\text{HCN}$ to give the $\text{C-OH}$ product and regenerate $\text{CN}^-$.
$$\text{R}_2\text{C(CN)O}^- + \text{HCN} \rightarrow \text{R}_2\text{C(CN)OH} + \text{CN}^-$$
Because $\text{CN}^-$ is regenerated, it acts as a catalyst. Pure $\text{HCN}$ alone reacts far too slowly, so a source of $\text{CN}^-$ such as $\text{KCN}$ is added.

**Conclude the correct statement**

Only the statement about needing cyanide ions as a catalyst correctly describes this reaction.

options.A: Incorrect. The product is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{C(OH)(CN)CH}_2\text{CH}_3$. The central carbon has two identical ethyl groups, so it has only three different types of group and is achiral. Students often assume every cyanohydrin has a chiral centre, but symmetry here removes it.
options.B: Incorrect. Addition to a carbonyl is nucleophilic addition. The nucleophile $\text{CN}^-$ attacks the delta positive carbonyl carbon. Electrophilic addition is typical of alkenes, not carbonyls.
options.C: Incorrect. The first intermediate after $\text{CN}^-$ attack is an alkoxide ion, $\text{R}_2\text{C(CN)O}^-$. The $\text{C-OH}$ group only forms in the second step after protonation by $\text{HCN}$.
options.D: Correct. $\text{HCN}$ is a weak acid and poor nucleophile source on its own. A small amount of $\text{CN}^-$ (from $\text{NaCN}$ or $\text{KCN}$) is added to attack the carbonyl, and it is regenerated when $\text{HCN}$ protonates the alkoxide intermediate, so it is a catalyst.
